title: Wonder Bets Big on Indian Food With Dabba — Can Desi Cuisine Finally Go Chain-Scale?
excerpt: The $2 billion food-hall giant launches an Indian concept inspired by Mumbai's dabbawalas, testing whether butter chicken can work at 100 locations.
body:
Wonder, the fast-growing food hall and delivery venture backed by more than $2 billion in private funding, has launched Dabba — a new Indian restaurant concept currently testing in four Philadelphia-area locations. The move puts a direct question to the American food industry: can Indian cuisine, with its complex spice profiles and labor-intensive cooking methods, scale the way pizza and burgers have?

What Is Dabba?

Named after Mumbai's legendary dabbawalas — the lunch delivery workers who have been navigating the city's chaotic streets for over 130 years — Dabba offers Indian staples including samosas ($8.95), chicken tikka masala, butter chicken ($19.95), and lamb vindaloo. The menu was developed by Wonder's in-house culinary team, which includes chefs with experience in Indian cuisine.

Wonder's model is vertically integrated: curries and sauces are developed in-house at a central facility, then shipped to storefronts where they are finished to order. Each Wonder location houses up to 30 restaurant brands, from pizza to sushi. Dabba joins this roster as part of a strategy to appeal to broad consumer tastes and reduce what the company calls "veto votes" — when one person in a group does not want a particular cuisine.

If the Philadelphia test succeeds, Dabba could roll out across Wonder's 100-plus East Coast storefronts, making it one of the largest Indian food operations in the United States.

The Scaling Problem

Indian food has long been considered one of the hardest cuisines to scale. The layering of spices, the variety of regional techniques, and the expectation of freshness have kept most Indian restaurants small and independent. The largest chains — Bawarchi Indian Cuisine with 50 locations, Honest Restaurants with 42, and Curry Up Now with 19 — are modest by fast-food standards.

"We've built a vertically integrated model that allows us to control the full process — from recipe development through production and final preparation in our kitchens," a Wonder spokesperson said. "For Dabba, that includes developing our curries and sauces in-house and focusing on the techniques required to build depth and consistency in flavor."

The four-store test is designed to refine recipes before a wider rollout. It is an approach that acknowledges the technical difficulty — you cannot simply open 100 Indian restaurants overnight.

Competition Is Heating Up

Wonder is not the only player eyeing Indian food at scale. Dishoom, London's cult-favorite Bombay café chain, is preparing to open its first American location in New York later this year, backed by private-equity firm L Catterton. Meanwhile, new independent concepts like Indienne (a Michelin-starred Chicago transplant now in Hudson Yards) and Drāvida (celebrity chef Aarthi Sampath's debut in the East Village) are raising the ceiling for what Indian dining can be in America.

The convergence is notable: at the same moment that fine-dining Indian restaurants are earning Michelin stars and James Beard nominations, a $2 billion delivery company is betting it can sell butter chicken at scale. Indian food is being pulled in both directions simultaneously — toward prestige and toward ubiquity.

What NRIs Should Watch

For the diaspora, this is a double-edged development. On one hand, seeing Indian food in a Wonder food hall alongside pizza and Thai noodles is a milestone of normalization. On the other hand, there are legitimate concerns about whether a centralized kitchen can do justice to a cuisine that many NRIs grew up watching their parents cook with intuition, not formulas.

The answer will come from Philadelphia first. If Dabba's butter chicken passes the taste test — not just for American palates, but for the desi families who know what it should taste like — then Indian food's American chapter is about to get much bigger.

What's Next

Wonder plans to expand Dabba systemwide later this year if the Philadelphia pilot succeeds, and the company will enter Texas in 2027. Founded by ecommerce entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder also owns Grubhub and Blue Apron and is eyeing an IPO in 2028. For Indian food in America, the stakes — and the funding — have never been higher.
